source_text: Illos ergo qui numquam nati sunt, bonos potuisse esse dicis, istos vero, qui mundum impleverunt, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, diaboli opus et de morbo natos et ab exordio reos definis. Probavi itaque nihil te aliud agere, quam ut Deum neges horum, qui sunt, hominum conditorem
pass_a_gloss: Those therefore who were never born you say could have been good, but these who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, you define as the devil's work and born from a disease and guilty from the beginning. I have therefore proved that you do nothing other than deny that God is the founder of these human beings who are.

lemmas.lexica: LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing

pass_b_english: You say, then, that those who were never born could have been good. But those who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, you declare to be the devil’s work, born from a disease, and guilty from the beginning. I have therefore proved that all you are doing is denying that God created the human beings who actually exist.

choices.why: Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, De nuptiis et concupiscentia 2 / On Marriage and Concupiscence); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
